script.opening: "This is horrible, doctor — when I open my bowels it’s an agonising sharp pain, like passing glass or razor blades, and then it throbs for ages afterwards. There’s bright red blood on the paper. I’ve been constipated since the baby. I’m almost scared to go now."

facts.text: Started about 3 weeks after the birth (baby, Mateo, now 7 weeks). Sharp, tearing pain every time she opens her bowels, then a deep throbbing ache "for an hour or two afterwards". Has started putting off going.
Bright red, a streak on the paper and on the outside of the stool. Not mixed in, no clots, not dark. Small amounts.
Before pregnancy, daily and normal. Now hard stools every 3–4 days. No diarrhoea, no mucus, no urgency. No lump hanging down. No itch.
No weight loss (apart from after the birth), no tummy pain, no fever, no mouth ulcers, no joint pains, no night sweats. No family history of bowel cancer or Crohn’s or colitis.

Normal vaginal delivery with a small tear that was stitched; healed. Breastfeeding. Not drinking enough — "maybe 4 glasses of water a day". Takes nothing for it. No regular medicines; stopped her pregnancy iron tablets after the birth. No allergies.
Tired, "fed up with this", but enjoying the baby; no low mood if asked. Partner, Luis, is supportive. Second child; older daughter is 4.

Embarrassed but determined to get help. Ask "So it’s not piles?" and "Why does feeding matter?" if breastfeeding is asked about. Relieved when it’s explained clearly. Would rather not be examined today if it can be avoided, but would accept an examination at the surgery if needed.

ice.ideas: "I thought it was piles from the pregnancy."
ice.concerns: "That something’s really wrong down there — the blood frightened me." She is avoiding going to the toilet.
ice.expectations: "Something to stop the pain, and to know what it is."

cues: "I’m almost scared to go now" — the pain–constipation cycle.
"Since the baby" — postnatal constipation and low fluid intake.
"Why does feeding matter?" — breastfeeding affects which treatments are suitable.

checkpoints.text: Recognises ANAL FISSURE — severe sharp pain on defecation with lingering spasm, bright red bleeding, and a posterior-midline tear, precipitated by constipation/postpartum — examining gently with a chaperone offered and without forcing a digital rectal examination
Distinguishes it from haemorrhoids (usually painless bleeding) using the severe-pain pattern

Recognises that ATYPICAL fissures (lateral, multiple, non-healing) warrant thinking about IBD/Crohn’s, infection or malignancy — screening GI/systemic symptoms and considering referral, and applies NICE NG12 with FIT (NICE HTG690) for blood mixed with stool, bowel change, weight loss or anaemia

Makes treating CONSTIPATION/optimising stool the cornerstone (fluids, gradual fibre, an osmotic laxative titrated to soft stools) to break the pain–spasm cycle, with analgesia, a short course of topical lidocaine and sitz baths

Considers a topical sphincter relaxant only for persistent or chronic fissures — Rectogesic (licensed for pain; not with PDE-5 inhibitors; not in pregnancy; not recommended when breastfeeding, MHRA SPC) or unlicensed diltiazem 2% — and refers to colorectal for chronic/non-healing fissures or red flags/atypical features
Reassures that most fissures heal with stool softening, addresses the fear of defecation, and checks understanding
Explains the diagnosis and management sensitively, asks about breastfeeding before prescribing, counsels GTN headache if used, and asks about postnatal mood

Safety-nets and follows up: review at 6–8 weeks, escalate if not healing (topical relaxant → colorectal), and reconsider/refer for atypical/non-healing fissures or red flags — constipation management as the cornerstone

worked.txt: "That ‘passing glass’ pain with bright blood is a classic anal fissure — a small tear, usually from constipation and straining, very common after having a baby. The bright blood on the paper fits, and the good news is most heal well."

"The single most important treatment is keeping your stool soft so it stops re-tearing and you’re not straining — plenty of fluids and fibre, and a stool-softening laxative that I’ll check suits you if you’re breastfeeding. That breaks the cycle of pain making you avoid going."
"For the pain, a local anaesthetic gel before you go, for a short time, and warm sitz baths help relax the area and ease the spasm. Try not to dread going — softer stools make it much more bearable."

"If it doesn’t settle, I’ll see you in 6 to 8 weeks and we can consider an ointment that relaxes the muscle to ease the pain. The usual one, GTN, often causes headaches, isn’t used in pregnancy and isn’t recommended when breastfeeding, so we’d choose between that and an alternative called diltiazem, which isn’t licensed for this, together."
"If it stays stubborn, I’d refer to the bowel surgeons, who have other options. And if a fissure is in an unusual position, there are several, or it won’t heal, I’d look into other causes."

"Come back if it’s not settling with stool softening, the bleeding changes (darker, mixed in the stool, or a lot), or you get other bowel symptoms or weight loss — then I’d want to investigate further."

f.learning: ANAL FISSURE presents with SEVERE SHARP PAIN on defecation (classically "passing glass/razor blades") with a lingering throb/sphincter spasm afterwards and BRIGHT RED blood on the paper or stool surface, usually from a tear in the POSTERIOR MIDLINE precipitated by hard stool/CONSTIPATION or occurring POSTPARTUM — with the painful defecation and fear of going being characteristic; examine gently, face to face with a chaperone offered (full PR is often too painful and should not be forced, but inspection may reveal the fissure/sentinel tag; arrange review if the examination is incomplete). Acute fissures are under 6 weeks; chronic 6 weeks or more. Distinguish it from HAEMORRHOIDS, which usually cause painless bright bleeding. Importantly, ATYPICAL fissures (lateral position, multiple, non-healing, or with other features) should prompt consideration of underlying disease — inflammatory bowel disease/Crohn’s (perianal disease), infection (HIV, syphilis, TB), trauma and rarely malignancy — so screen GI/systemic symptoms and consider referral/further assessment for atypical or non-healing fissures. The cornerstone of management is treating CONSTIPATION/optimising stool: adequate fluids, fibre increased gradually where appropriate (fibre without enough fluid can make things worse) and an osmotic laxative titrated to soft stools if they stay hard (dose per BNF), continued after healing, to keep stool soft and avoid straining (breaking the pain–constipation–spasm cycle), with analgesia, a short course of topical lidocaine and sitz baths for relief — most acute fissures heal with stool softening. For persistent or chronic fissures, consider a topical sphincter relaxant: Rectogesic (GTN 0.4%) is licensed for pain in chronic anal fissure (every 12 hours for up to 8 weeks; the SPC reports no statistically significant healing benefit over placebo; headache very common; not with PDE-5 inhibitors or other nitrates; do not use in pregnancy; not recommended when breastfeeding, MHRA SPC), and diltiazem 2% is an unlicensed alternative twice daily for about 6–8 weeks (local formulary). Review at 6–8 weeks and refer to colorectal surgery for chronic/non-healing or recurrent fissures (the specialist chooses between botulinum toxin and sphincter surgery) or red flags/atypical features. Reassure that most heal, address the fear of defecation, ask about postnatal mood (NICE CG192), and safety-net. A fissure does not exclude other pathology: blood mixed with stool, a persistent change in bowel habit, weight loss, iron-deficiency anaemia or a mass need assessment under NICE NG12, with FIT where indicated (NICE HTG690); a rectal or anal mass or unexplained anal ulceration → consider a suspected cancer pathway referral.

knowledge.summary: Severe, sharp pain on passing stool with a throbbing ache afterwards and bright red blood on the paper, after postnatal constipation, is an anal fissure. The foundation is keeping stools soft; a topical sphincter relaxant is for persistent or chronic fissures, and its pregnancy and breastfeeding cautions matter in a postnatal woman.

points.t: Severe pain on or after defecation, often lasting minutes to hours, with bright red blood on the paper, usually from a posterior midline tear after hard stool. Acute: under 6 weeks. Chronic: 6 weeks or more, often with a sentinel tag or indurated edges. Inspect gently; do not force a digital rectal examination when it is too painful, but arrange review if the examination is incomplete.

Haemorrhoids usually bleed painlessly unless thrombosed. A lateral, multiple, painless, indurated, large or non-healing fissure means reconsidering the diagnosis: Crohn’s disease, HIV, TB, syphilis, malignancy or trauma.

Fluids, gradual fibre where appropriate, and an osmotic laxative if stools stay hard, titrated to soft stools (dose per BNF). Fibre without enough fluid can make things worse. Avoid straining and continue after healing. Warm baths ease spasm; a short course of topical lidocaine before defecation for severe pain (BNF).

For a persistent or chronic fissure: Rectogesic (GTN 0.4%) is licensed for pain in chronic anal fissure, applied intra-anally every 12 hours for up to 8 weeks [1]. Headache is very common. Not with PDE-5 inhibitors or other nitrates; do not use in pregnancy; not recommended when breastfeeding [1]. Diltiazem 2% is an unlicensed alternative, used twice daily for about 6–8 weeks.

Colorectal surgery if not healed after about 6–8 weeks of stool softening and topical treatment, if recurrent, or if atypical. The surgeon chooses between botulinum toxin and sphincter surgery, weighing continence and obstetric history.

A fissure does not exclude other pathology. Blood mixed with stool, a persistent change in bowel habit, weight loss, iron-deficiency anaemia or a mass need assessment under NICE NG12 [2], using FIT where indicated (NICE HTG690 [3]). A rectal or anal mass or unexplained anal ulceration: consider a suspected cancer pathway referral.
Postnatal constipation, fear of opening the bowels and sleep loss often coexist. NICE CG192 [4]: consider asking about low mood and anxiety in the postnatal period.

Review at 6–8 weeks; colorectal referral if not healing; red-flag and mood safety-net.

Idea (something wrong down there), concern (the blood), expectation (relief and an explanation).
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.

model.text: Hello Mrs Reyes, I’m Dr Patel. How can I help today?

This is horrible, doctor. When I open my bowels it’s an agonising sharp pain, like passing glass or razor blades, and then it throbs for ages afterwards. There’s bright red blood on the paper. I’ve been constipated since the baby. I’m almost scared to go now.
That sounds really painful, and I can see why you’re dreading it. Let me ask a few questions and then we can sort out a plan.
How long has the pain been going on?
Since not long after the baby. I haven’t counted the weeks.
Is the blood on the paper and on the outside of the stool, or mixed in with it? Is it bright red or darker?
Bright red, on the paper and a bit on the outside. Not mixed in.
Apart from the constipation, has your bowel pattern changed? Any tummy pain, diarrhoea, weight loss or tiredness beyond what a new baby brings?
No, just hard and not often. I’m tired, but that’s the baby.
Do you feel a lump coming down, or is it mainly pain?
No lump. It’s the pain.
What are you drinking and eating at the moment? Have you tried anything for the constipation?
Not enough water, to be honest. I haven’t taken anything.
Are you taking any medicines, and are you breastfeeding? Both affect what I can prescribe.
model.why: Medication and breastfeeding check before prescribing

model.text: No regular medicines. Why does feeding matter?
Some treatments aren’t recommended when breastfeeding, so I’ll choose with that in mind whichever way you’re feeding.
Having a new baby and pain like this is a lot. How are you feeling in yourself?
Tired and fed up with this. Otherwise okay, I think.
What worried you most about the blood?
That something’s really wrong down there.

I’d like to have a gentle look, just from the outside. I won’t put a finger inside if it’s too painful. Would you like a chaperone? (With consent: gentle parting of the buttocks shows a small posterior midline tear. No lump, no lateral or multiple tears. Examination stopped there.)
model.why: Consent, chaperone, gentle inspection only; checks for atypical features

model.text: You have an anal fissure, a small tear in the lining at the back of the back passage. Hard stools caused it, and the muscle there goes into spasm, which is the throbbing afterwards. The spasm and the fear of going make the stools harder, so it becomes a cycle. It’s in the usual place, and the bleeding fits, so it doesn’t look like anything more serious.
model.why: Names the diagnosis, explains the cycle, addresses her fear

model.text: So it’s not piles?
Piles usually bleed without much pain. This severe pain is typical of a fissure.

The most important treatment is keeping your stools soft so the tear can heal. More water, fibre built up gradually, and a laxative that softens the stool. I’ll check it suits you if you’re breastfeeding. Adjust the dose so stools are soft but not runny, and keep going even after it heals.
And for the pain?
A numbing gel before you open your bowels, for a short time, and a warm bath afterwards relaxes the muscle. Most of these heal with this alone.
model.why: Short topical anaesthetic and warm baths

model.text: What if it doesn’t heal?

Then there’s an ointment to relax the muscle. The usual one often gives headaches, and it isn’t used in pregnancy and isn’t recommended when breastfeeding, so we’d choose between that and an alternative together. If it still doesn’t heal, I’d refer you to the bowel surgeons.
model.why: Stepped plan with GTN cautions in a postnatal woman

model.text: Come back if the blood becomes mixed in with the stool or dark, if your bowels change, you lose weight, or you get a painful swelling or fever near the back passage. I’ll see you in 6 to 8 weeks, or sooner if it’s not easing. What will you do when you get home?
model.why: Specific red flags, review interval and teach-back

model.text: Drink more, take the softener every day, use the gel before I go, and come back if the bleeding changes.
Perfect. And if your mood dips, please tell us. You don’t need to struggle on.

social.t: Sleep loss, little time to eat and drink, and fear of pain all worsen constipation. Practical, small steps work best.
The health visitor can support her and ask about mood and feeding.

legal.t: Diltiazem 2% is unlicensed for anal fissure. Explain this and record the discussion (GMC good practice in prescribing).
Explain, gain consent, offer a chaperone and record it (GMC).

professional.t: Check the BNF for each medicine. Rectogesic is not recommended when breastfeeding and must not be used in pregnancy (MHRA SPC).
If the examination is incomplete or features are atypical, arrange review or referral rather than assuming a simple fissure.

community.t: Community pharmacists can advise on laxatives and simple measures, and on whether a product is suitable when breastfeeding.
The 6–8 week postnatal check is a chance to review healing, bowels and mood.

redFlags: Blood mixed with stool or dark blood
Persistent change in bowel habit, weight loss or iron-deficiency anaemia (NICE NG12; FIT per NICE HTG690)
Lateral, multiple, painless or non-healing fissure
Painful swelling, fever or discharge near the anus (abscess)
psychosocial: New baby, tiredness and low fluid intake
ice: Concern: the bright blood and the pain

playbook.diagnosis: “This is an anal fissure, a small tear at the back of the back passage, caused by hard stools.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “The tear hurts when stool passes, then the muscle around it tightens and throbs. That makes you hold on, stools get harder, and it tears again. Soft stools break that cycle.”

management.reflectIce: “You were worried something was seriously wrong. The tear is in the typical place and the bleeding fits, which is reassuring, and I’ll review you to make sure it heals.”
management.psychosocial: Acknowledge the dread of going and the demands of a new baby; ask about mood.
sharedPlan: Fluids, gradual fibre and an osmotic laxative titrated to soft stools (BNF); continue after healing
Short course of topical lidocaine before defecation; warm baths
If persistent at 6–8 weeks: topical relaxant, with GTN cautions in pregnancy and breastfeeding (MHRA SPC) or unlicensed diltiazem; colorectal referral if still not healed
safetyNet: Blood mixed with stool, dark blood, bowel change or weight loss: return for assessment
Painful swelling, fever or discharge near the anus: urgent review
Low mood or anxiety: contact the practice or health visitor

pitfalls.intro: This station rewards a confident diagnosis and a stool-first plan. Marks are lost by calling it piles, by forcing an examination, and by prescribing GTN without checking breastfeeding.

items.why: Severe pain on defecation with bright blood on the paper points to a fissure; haemorrhoids usually bleed painlessly.
items.fix: Name the fissure and explain the difference.

items.why: Stool softening is the foundation; GTN is for persistent or chronic fissures, often causes headache, and is not recommended when breastfeeding (MHRA SPC).
items.fix: Start with an osmotic laxative, lidocaine and warm baths; review at 6–8 weeks.

items.why: It is very painful with an acute fissure and gentle inspection is usually enough.
items.fix: Inspect gently; if incomplete, arrange review rather than assuming it is simple.

items.fail: Not checking for red flags or atypical features.
items.why: Blood mixed with stool, bowel change, weight loss or an atypical fissure change the pathway (NICE NG12).
items.fix: Ask directly and safety-net with named symptoms.

items.fail: Ignoring the fear of going and the new baby.
items.why: Fear drives the constipation, and postnatal mood matters (NICE CG192).
items.fix: Explain the cycle and ask how she is coping.

items.why: Healing needs checking at 6–8 weeks before stepping up or referring.
items.fix: Book review and say when colorectal referral would follow.

wordPics.pass: Recognises an anal fissure, examines gently, makes stool softening the foundation with pain relief, and safety-nets for red flags.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: explains the pain–spasm cycle in plain words; checks breastfeeding before prescribing and knows GTN is not recommended; asks about postnatal mood; names the 6–8 week review and the colorectal route; confirms the plan by teach-back.

avoid.instead: “Severe pain on going with bright blood is a small tear called a fissure.”
avoid.why: Mislabelling leads to the wrong advice and ignores the pain.

avoid.dont: “I’ll just have a quick feel inside.”
avoid.instead: “I’ll look gently from the outside and won’t examine inside if it’s too painful.”
avoid.why: Forcing a DRE on an acute fissure is painful and unnecessary; arrange review if the examination is incomplete.

avoid.dont: “Put this GTN ointment on twice a day.”
avoid.instead: “Softening your stools comes first. If it doesn’t heal, we’ll look at an ointment, checking it’s safe with feeding.”
avoid.why: GTN is for persistent or chronic fissures and is not recommended when breastfeeding (MHRA SPC).

Blood mixed with stool, a persistent change in bowel habit, weight loss, iron-deficiency anaemia or a mass need assessment under NICE NG12 [2], using FIT where indicated (NICE HTG690 [3]). A rectal or anal mass or unexplained anal ulceration: consider a suspected cancer pathway referral.
Postnatal constipation, fear of opening the bowels and sleep loss often coexist. NICE CG192 [4]: consider asking about low mood and anxiety in the postnatal period.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Open start; let her describe the pain, bleeding and fear of going.
New baby, tiredness, fluid intake and postnatal mood explored.
Picked up “scared to go” and explained the pain–spasm–constipation cycle.
Idea (something wrong down there), concern (the blood), expectation (relief and an explanation).
Chaperone; gentle external inspection without a forced DRE; atypical features looked for; review if examination incomplete.
Fissure versus haemorrhoids, atypical fissure (Crohn’s, infection, malignancy) and colorectal causes.
Asked about blood mixed with stool, bowel change, weight loss; NICE NG12 and FIT (NICE HTG690) if these develop.
Named an anal fissure, posterior midline, typical.
Stool softening with an osmotic laxative, short topical lidocaine, warm baths; topical relaxant only if persistent, with GTN cautions (MHRA SPC).
Breastfeeding status checked before prescribing; postnatal mood asked (NICE CG192).
Review at 6–8 weeks; colorectal referral if not healing; red-flag and mood safety-net.

social.t: Sleep loss, little time to eat and drink, and fear of pain all worsen constipation. Practical, small steps work best.
The health visitor can support her and ask about mood and feeding.

legal.t: Diltiazem 2% is unlicensed for anal fissure. Explain this and record the discussion (GMC good practice in prescribing).
Explain, gain consent, offer a chaperone and record it (GMC).

professional.t: Check the BNF for each medicine. Rectogesic is not recommended when breastfeeding and must not be used in pregnancy (MHRA SPC).
If the examination is incomplete or features are atypical, arrange review or referral rather than assuming a simple fissure.

community.t: Community pharmacists can advise on laxatives and simple measures, and on whether a product is suitable when breastfeeding.
The 6–8 week postnatal check is a chance to review healing, bowels and mood.

redFlags: Blood mixed with stool or dark blood
Persistent change in bowel habit, weight loss or iron-deficiency anaemia (NICE NG12; FIT per NICE HTG690)
Lateral, multiple, painless or non-healing fissure
Painful swelling, fever or discharge near the anus (abscess)
psychosocial: New baby, tiredness and low fluid intake
ice: Concern: the bright blood and the pain

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: “This is an anal fissure, a small tear at the back of the back passage, caused by hard stools.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “The tear hurts when stool passes, then the muscle around it tightens and throbs. That makes you hold on, stools get harder, and it tears again. Soft stools break that cycle.”

management.reflectIce: “You were worried something was seriously wrong. The tear is in the typical place and the bleeding fits, which is reassuring, and I’ll review you to make sure it heals.”
management.psychosocial: Acknowledge the dread of going and the demands of a new baby; ask about mood.
sharedPlan: Fluids, gradual fibre and an osmotic laxative titrated to soft stools (BNF); continue after healing
Short course of topical lidocaine before defecation; warm baths
If persistent at 6–8 weeks: topical relaxant, with GTN cautions in pregnancy and breastfeeding (MHRA SPC) or unlicensed diltiazem; colorectal referral if still not healed
safetyNet: Blood mixed with stool, dark blood, bowel change or weight loss: return for assessment
Painful swelling, fever or discharge near the anus: urgent review
Low mood or anxiety: contact the practice or health visitor

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station rewards a confident diagnosis and a stool-first plan. Marks are lost by calling it piles, by forcing an examination, and by prescribing GTN without checking breastfeeding.

items.why: Severe pain on defecation with bright blood on the paper points to a fissure; haemorrhoids usually bleed painlessly.
items.fix: Name the fissure and explain the difference.

items.why: Stool softening is the foundation; GTN is for persistent or chronic fissures, often causes headache, and is not recommended when breastfeeding (MHRA SPC).
items.fix: Start with an osmotic laxative, lidocaine and warm baths; review at 6–8 weeks.

items.why: It is very painful with an acute fissure and gentle inspection is usually enough.
items.fix: Inspect gently; if incomplete, arrange review rather than assuming it is simple.

items.fail: Not checking for red flags or atypical features.
items.why: Blood mixed with stool, bowel change, weight loss or an atypical fissure change the pathway (NICE NG12).
items.fix: Ask directly and safety-net with named symptoms.

items.fail: Ignoring the fear of going and the new baby.
items.why: Fear drives the constipation, and postnatal mood matters (NICE CG192).
items.fix: Explain the cycle and ask how she is coping.

items.why: Healing needs checking at 6–8 weeks before stepping up or referring.
items.fix: Book review and say when colorectal referral would follow.
